question: In Sweden, mobile EU citizens are asked to prove their right to stay in the country for at least one year to obtain a personal identification number (‘personnummer’), which is necessary to exercise basic rights and access essential services.

This requirement leads to many EU citizens being prevented from obtaining a registration certificate, contributing to destitution among those newcomers who cannot obtain year-long work contracts. In 2023, a solution to issue a ‘coordination number’ for those with job contracts shorter than one year was implemented, but in practice this has a much more limited scope than the personal identification number.

A complaint was submitted to the Commission in 2017 on this matter (CHAP(2017)03524)1. The meeting of Parliament’s Committee on Petitions (PETI) on 23 October 2023 discussed as many as thirteen petitions related to problems with issuing the ‘personnummer’ for mobile EU citizens2. 1.
Does the Commission acknowledge this is an additional requirement not set out in Directive 2004/38/EC3, hampering the right of mobile EU citizens to reside in Sweden?
Will the Commission start an investigation to make sure there are no breaches of EU law in Sweden’s transposition of the abovementioned Directive?
answer: On 1 September 2023, Sweden adopted a new law on Coordination Numbers (Lag om samordningsnummer, 2022:1697), strengthening identity verification in order for Coordination Numbers (CNs) to be more reliable and to be accepted as Personal Identification Numbers (PINs).

According to the information received from the Swedish authorities, the new law makes it possible to use a ‘confirmed’ CN in the same way as a PIN and can therefore allow individuals access to the same services. A ‘confirmed’ CN is issued to persons who have proven their identity and, to this end individuals must show up in person for the identity check.

EU citizens can now apply for a CN by themselves if they prove a connection with Sweden (there is no longer a residence requirement). In addition, other alternatives exist for access to services. Based on Regulation (EU) No 910/2014, EU citizens should be entitled to access Swedish online public services using electronic identification means issued pursuant to a notified scheme in another Member State.

Not all Member States have notified an electronic identification scheme (4). Rules amending that regulation will entitle all EU citizens to identify themselves online and offline seamlessly across borders for public and private services through European Digital Identity Wallets, to be developed by 2026 (5).
The Commission has been in regular contacts with the Swedish authorities on that matter and will continue monitoring the application of the new law on CNs in Sweden.
